layers.name: Vector index / ANN
layers.measures: Does the index return the true nearest neighbours fast and cheaply?

layers.name: Retrieval quality
layers.measures: Are the right passages in the context, and ranked high?

layers.name: Generation quality
layers.measures: Is the answer correct, supported by the context, on topic, and robust?

layers.name: GraphRAG-specific
layers.measures: Is the graph right, does graph retrieval fetch the multi-hop evidence, and is the build cost worth it?

layers.name: System
layers.measures: How fast and how expensive is one answer, and how many can we serve?

layers.name: Education-specific

layers.name: Reporting and reliability

units.name: Recall@k vs exact kNN
units.question: Of the k true nearest neighbours, how many did the approximate index return?
units.symbols: A_k = ids returned by the ANN index for query q; T_k = ids of the exact top-k (brute force); p*_k = the k-th true neighbour; d = distance. The distance form (used by ann-benchmarks) counts ties as correct.

inputs.other: exact kNN ground truth for the same vectors and queries (brute force), no relevance labels

worked_example.setup: k=10. Exact top-10 ids: 1..10. The index returns 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,11,12.

units.blind_spots: Measures only fidelity to exact search, not whether the neighbours are relevant to a human. A perfect index over a bad embedding scores 1.0. Averaging hides bad queries (look at the per-query minimum). Depends on k, on the distance, and on tie handling.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use it to tune the index (ef_search, nprobe). Use Precision@k / nDCG against labels to judge the whole retrieval. Qdrant FineWeb-10B ships exact top-1000 ground truth so you can measure recall@10 and recall@100 at depth.

source.cite: Aumüller, Bernhardsson, Faithfull 2020, ANN-Benchmarks, Information Systems 87

units.notes: ann-benchmarks definition verified in the paper text (distance-based recall and (1+eps)-recall). Filtered search needs ground truth computed under the same filter (Qdrant FineWeb-10B provides it).

units.name: Queries per second (QPS)
units.question: How many queries can the index answer per second at a given recall?
units.symbols: Q = number of queries; T_total = wall-clock seconds to answer all of them under the stated hardware and thread count.

inputs.other: query set, one fixed machine, fixed thread count, warm cache

worked_example.setup: 10,000 queries run in 4.0 s on one CPU thread.

units.blind_spots: Meaningless without the recall at which it was measured. Depends on hardware, threads, batch mode, filter selectivity and whether the data is in RAM. ann-benchmarks runs one CPU thread by default (verified), cloud benchmarks often do not.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Always plot QPS against recall (see the trade-off curve). Use latency percentiles when users wait for each answer; QPS when you care about throughput under load.

source.cite: Aumüller, Bernhardsson, Faithfull 2020, ANN-Benchmarks, Information Systems 87

units.name: Latency percentiles p50 / p95 / p99
units.question: How long does one query take for a typical user, and how long for the unlucky ones?
units.formula_latex: p_q=x_{(\lceil qn\rceil)}\quad\text{(nearest rank on the sorted latencies }x_{(1)}\le\dots\le x_{(n)})
units.symbols: x_(i) = i-th smallest of n measured latencies; q = 0.5, 0.95 or 0.99.

inputs.other: per-query latency log

units.blind_spots: Needs enough samples: p99 from 20 points is just the maximum. Coordinated omission (a closed-loop test that waits for slow replies) under-reports the tail. Percentiles of stages do not add up.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use p50 for the typical case, p95/p99 for service goals (the Qdrant blog quotes sub-100 ms p99). Use QPS for throughput.

source.cite: NumPy 2.3.3 numpy.percentile(method='inverted_cdf') = Hyndman & Fan method 1 = nearest rank
source.where: numpy/lib/_function_base_impl.py, function _inverted_cdf (virtual index n*q-1, gamma==0): returns the ceil(n*q)-th order statistic

units.name: Index build time and ingest rate
units.question: How long does it take to build or update the index, and how fast can we ingest vectors?
units.symbols: N = number of vectors indexed; T_build = seconds it took to build the index (ANN-Benchmarks, Table 1). The ingest rate N/T_build is our derived quantity, not defined in the paper; if you count optimiser/segment-merge time (Qdrant), say so.

inputs.other: build log with timestamps; same hardware

units.higher_is_better: lower for time, higher for rate

worked_example.setup: 1,000,000 vectors indexed in 500 s.

units.blind_spots: Depends on the build parameters (HNSW M, ef_construct), on CPU count and on whether optimisation after upload is counted. A fast build with low recall is not a win.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Matters for large or frequently changing corpora. For a fixed textbook corpus of tens of thousands of chunks it is seconds and not a decision driver.

source.cite: Aumuller, Bernhardsson, Faithfull 2020, ANN-Benchmarks, Information Systems 87
source.where: Sec. 2.1 'Quality Measures', Table 1 (PDF p. 4): 'Index build time DS - Time it took to build DS (in seconds)'; 'Index size of DS' in kB

superseded.text: N = number of vectors indexed; T_build = seconds until the index can serve at its target recall.

units.name: Index memory (bytes per vector)
units.question: How much RAM or disk does the index need per stored vector?
units.formula_latex: B_{\mathrm{vec}}=\frac{M_{\mathrm{index}}}{N}\;\approx\; d\cdot b_{\mathrm{dtype}}+(M_{\max0}+m_L\,M_{\max})\cdot b_{\mathrm{link}},\quad M_{\max0}=2M,\ M_{\max}=M,\ m_L=1/\ln M
units.symbols: M_index = resident memory of the index minus the empty process; N = vectors; d = dimension; b_dtype = bytes per component (4 for float32, 2 for float16, 1 for int8); M = HNSW links parameter; M_max0 = max links on layer 0 (2M by default); M_max = max links on upper layers (M); m_L = level-generation factor (1/ln M); b_link = bytes per link (4: 4-byte unsigned int, up to ~4 billion elements).

inputs.other: process memory before and after load

worked_example.setup: N = 1,000,000 vectors, d = 768, float32; HNSW with M = 16 (layer 0 keeps up to 2M = 32 links of 4 bytes).
worked_example.steps: Raw vectors: 768 x 4 = 3,072 B each. Layer-0 links: 2M = 32 links x 4 B = 128 B. Upper layers: m_L*M_max = (1/ln 16)*16 = 5.77 links x 4 B = 23 B. Total 3,072 + 128 + 23 = 3,223 B, about 3,200 B per vector, so about 3.2 GB for 1 M vectors. Qdrant FineWeb-10B for scale: 24.47 TB of vectors / 10.07 B documents = about 2,430 B per document (dense 768-d half precision = 1,536 B plus sparse); Qdrant figures not re-checked.

units.blind_spots: Counts only what you measure: payload, quantisation, replicas and the OS cache change the answer. The link count formula is the textbook HNSW layout (unverified against the Qdrant implementation).
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use it with recall: quantisation cuts memory 4x at some recall cost. Decide RAM vs disk index by this number, not by QPS alone.

source.cite: Malkov & Yashunin 2018, HNSW, IEEE TPAMI 42(4); memory-measurement method from ANN-Benchmarks (Aumuller et al. 2020)
source.where: HNSW Sec. 4.2.3 'Memory cost' (PDF p. 8): average memory per element = (Mmax0 + mL*Mmax) * bytes_per_link; Mmax0 = 2*M suggested (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 6), mL = 1/ln(M) (Sec. 4.1). ANN-Benchmarks Sec. 3: memory = process memory after minus before initialising the index (matches the symbol M_index)

superseded.text: M_index = resident memory of the index minus the empty process; N = vectors; d = dimension; b_dtype = bytes per component (4 for float32, 2 for float16, 1 for int8).

Raw vectors: 768 x 4 = 3,072 B each. Links: 32 x 4 = 128 B each. Total about 3,200 B per vector, so 3.2 GB for 1 M vectors. Qdrant FineWeb-10B for scale: 24.47 TB of vectors / 10.07 B documents = about 2,430 B per document (dense 768-d half precision = 1,536 B plus sparse).

units.name: Recall-latency (recall-QPS) trade-off curve
units.question: At each recall level, what is the best speed we can get, and which settings are never worth using?
units.symbols: Each parameter setting i gives a point (rho_i = recall@k, s_i = QPS). The Pareto frontier is the set of non-dominated points.

inputs.other: a sweep over search parameters (e.g. ef_search), each run measured for recall and QPS

worked_example.steps: C is dominated by B (same recall, lower QPS). E is dominated by D (lower recall, lower QPS). Frontier = A, B, D.

units.blind_spots: A frontier of one dataset and one machine does not transfer. Plots with a log QPS axis hide big gaps. Do not compare engines tuned differently.
units.use_vs_neighbours: This is the headline plot of ann-benchmarks. Use a single point (recall@10 = 0.95) for a short report; the whole curve when choosing an index.

source.cite: Aumüller, Bernhardsson, Faithfull 2020, ANN-Benchmarks, Information Systems 87

units.name: Precision@k
units.question: Of the k passages we retrieved, how many are relevant?
units.symbols: Ret_k = the top-k retrieved items; Rel = the set of relevant items for the query (gold).

worked_example.setup: A query has 3 relevant documents {d1, d3, d4}. The system returns the ranking [d3, d7, d1, d9, d2]. k = 5.
worked_example.steps: Relevant in the top 5: d3 and d1 = 2. P@5 = 2/5.

units.blind_spots: Ignores order inside the top k and ignores relevant items that were never retrieved. Max is below 1 whenever |Rel| < k.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use when the reader sees all k passages (a tutor prompt). Use Recall@k when missing evidence is the risk, nDCG when relevance is graded.

source.cite: Manning, Raghavan, Schutze 2008, IIR ch. 8; trec_eval v10.0 m_P.c
source.where: IIR Sec. 8.3 (Precision = tp/(tp+fp)) and Sec. 8.4 'precision at k'; trec_eval m_P.c te_calc_P: value = rel_so_far / cutoff (divides by k even when fewer than k documents were returned)

units.name: Recall@k
units.question: Of all the relevant passages, how many made it into the top k?
units.symbols: Same symbols as Precision@k.

worked_example.setup: A query has 3 relevant documents {d1, d3, d4}. The system returns the ranking [d3, d7, d1, d9, d2]. k = 5.
worked_example.steps: Found d1 and d3 of {d1, d3, d4}: 2/3.

units.blind_spots: Rewards a long list: R@k rises with k even if the top is junk. Needs the full list of relevant items, which is hard to label on a big corpus (unlabelled relevant items count as misses).
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use it to ask 'is the evidence even in the context window?'. It upper-bounds what generation can do. Pair it with Precision@k to see the cost of a longer context.

source.cite: Manning, Raghavan, Schutze 2008, IIR ch. 8; trec_eval v10.0 m_recall.c
source.where: IIR Sec. 8.3 (Recall = tp/(tp+fn)); trec_eval m_recall.c te_calc_recall: value = rel_so_far / num_rel (num_rel = all relevant docs in the qrels; returns 0 if num_rel = 0)

units.name: Hit rate@k (success@k)
units.question: Did at least one relevant passage appear in the top k?
units.symbols: Q = set of queries; 1[.] = 1 if the condition holds, else 0.

worked_example.setup: Four queries. Their top-5 lists contain a relevant item: yes, no, yes, yes.

units.blind_spots: Very forgiving: one hit is enough, even if the answer needs three facts. Saturates near 1 for large k.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Right metric when one passage is sufficient (single-hop factual QA). For multi-hop use all-hop recall instead.

source.cite: trec_eval v10.0 measure 'success' (Stephen Tomlinson); Manning et al. 2008 do NOT define it
source.where: m_success.c te_meas_success: 'Success (a relevant doc has been retrieved) measured at various doc level cutoffs'; default cutoffs 1,5,10; averaged over queries by the standard trec_eval mean

units.name: Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR)
units.question: How high does the first relevant passage appear, on average?
units.formula_latex: \mathrm{MRR}=\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q\in Q}\frac{1}{\mathrm{rank}_q},\quad \mathrm{rank}_q=\text{position of the first relevant item (}1/\mathrm{rank}_q=0\text{ if none)}
units.symbols: rank_q = 1-based position of the first relevant result for query q.

worked_example.setup: Four queries: first relevant at rank 1, rank 3, not found, rank 2.

units.blind_spots: Looks only at the first relevant item; ignores the others. Steep: rank 2 gives 0.5, rank 10 gives 0.1.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use when the first good hit matters (a reranker, a single-passage prompt). Use MAP or nDCG when several relevant items matter.

source.cite: Voorhees 1999, The TREC-8 Question Answering Track Report, Proc. TREC-8, pp. 77-82
source.where: Voorhees 1999, Sec. 1 'The Task' (page 1, last paragraph): 'the score ... was mean reciprocal rank ... the reciprocal of the rank at which the first correct response was returned, or 0 if none of the five responses contained a correct answer'; trec_eval m_recip_rank.c: 1/(i+1) for the first relevant, otherwise 0

units.name: Mean Average Precision (MAP)
units.question: Are the relevant passages not only found but ranked near the top?
units.symbols: rel_k = 1 if the item at rank k is relevant, else 0; n = list length; |Rel| counts relevant items including those never retrieved.

worked_example.setup: A query has 3 relevant documents {d1, d3, d4}. The system returns the ranking [d3, d7, d1, d9, d2].
worked_example.steps: Relevant at rank 1 (P@1 = 1) and rank 3 (P@3 = 2/3). AP = (1 + 0.667) / 3 (the denominator is 3 because d4 was missed).

units.blind_spots: Binary relevance only. One number mixes ranking and coverage; hard to read what went wrong.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use when you have several relevant items per query and care about the whole ranking. nDCG is the graded version.

source.cite: Manning, Raghavan, Schutze 2008, IIR ch. 8 Eq. (43); trec_eval v10.0 m_map.c
source.where: IIR Sec. 8.4 Eq. (43): MAP(Q) = 1/|Q| sum_j 1/m_j sum_k Precision(R_jk), m_j = number of relevant documents; 'When a relevant document is not retrieved at all, the precision value in the above equation is taken to be 0'. trec_eval m_map.c: sum of (rel_so_far/(i+1)) over relevant ranks divided by num_rel

units.name: nDCG@k (graded relevance)
units.question: Is the ranking close to the best possible order when some passages are more relevant than others?
units.formula_latex: \mathrm{DCG@}k=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{g_i}{\log_2(i+1)},\quad \mathrm{nDCG@}k=\frac{\mathrm{DCG@}k}{\mathrm{IDCG@}k}\quad(\text{trec\_eval/BEIR convention; IIR Eq. 44 uses gain }2^{g_i}-1;\ \text{J\&K 2002 use }g_i/\log_b i\text{ only from rank }b)
units.symbols: g_i = graded relevance (e.g. 0 to 3) of the item at rank i; IDCG@k = DCG@k of the ideal ordering of ALL documents judged for the query (the recall base), cut at k, not only of the returned items (J&K Sec. 2.3; trec_eval). In the worked example the four returned items are all the judged ones, so both readings agree.

worked_example.setup: Top-4 grades in returned order: [3, 2, 0, 1]. Ideal order: [3, 2, 1, 0].

units.blind_spots: Needs graded labels. Two gain conventions (linear vs 2^g-1) give different numbers: state which. Unjudged items count as 0, so a system finding unlabelled relevant items is punished. Only about what is in the top k.
units.use_vs_neighbours: BEIR and MTEB report nDCG@10, so use it for embedding model choice and for comparing against published numbers. Use MAP for binary labels.

source.cite: Jarvelin & Kekalainen 2002, ACM TOIS 20(4), Eqs. (2), (4), Sec. 2.3; Manning et al. 2008, IIR Eq. (44); trec_eval v10.0 m_ndcg_cut.c
source.id: doi:10.1145/582415.582418 (read via faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~zha/CS8803WST/dcg.pdf, the TOIS pagination 422-446); https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/evaluation-of-ranked-retrieval-results-1.html; github.com/usnistgov/trec_eval
source.where: J&K Sec. 2.2 Eq. (2): DCG[i] = CG[i] if i < b, else DCG[i-1] + G[i]/log_b i (raw gain, no discount for ranks below the base b; b=2: ranks 1 and 2 are undiscounted); Sec. 2.3: ideal vector from ALL relevant documents of the request (Eq. 4). IIR Eq. (44): gain 2^R-1, denominator log2(1+m), Z_kj normalises a perfect ranking to 1. trec_eval m_ndcg_cut.c: gain/log2(i+2) for 0-based i (= log2(rank+1)), linear gain, ideal from all judged levels

superseded.text: g_i = graded relevance (e.g. 0 to 3) of the item at rank i; IDCG@k = DCG of the ideal ordering of the same items.

units.name: Context precision (RAGAS)
units.question: Are the relevant retrieved chunks ranked ahead of the irrelevant ones?
units.symbols: K = number of retrieved chunks; v_k in {0,1} = LLM verdict that chunk k is relevant to the question (given the reference answer or the generated answer); P@k = precision of the first k chunks.

worked_example.setup: 4 chunks; the judge says relevant: [1, 0, 1, 1].

units.blind_spots: Rank-aware average precision with an LLM instead of labels, so it inherits judge noise and variance. Says nothing about relevant chunks that were not retrieved.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use when you have no per-chunk gold labels but want a ranking-sensitive precision. Use real Precision@k / nDCG if you do have labels (cheaper and exact).

source.cite: Ragas v0.4.3 source code and docs (Es et al. 2024, RAGAS, does not define this metric)
source.where: src/ragas/metrics/_context_precision.py, LLMContextPrecisionWithReference._calculate_average_precision, lines 113-131 (numerator = sum_i [sum(v[:i+1])/(i+1)] * v_i; denominator = sum(v) + 1e-10); classes ContextPrecision (alias of ...WithReference, line 311) and ...WithoutReference (line 173); docs/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/context_precision.md Eq. for Context Precision@K

units.name: Context recall (RAGAS)
units.question: Does the retrieved context contain everything the reference answer says?
units.symbols: C_ref = claims (sentences) of the reference answer; attributable = the judge can find support for the claim in the retrieved text.

worked_example.setup: Reference answer has 4 claims; the judge finds support for 3 in the retrieved chunks.

units.blind_spots: Only as good as the reference answer. If the reference is incomplete the metric under-rewards extra useful context. A judge may accept loose paraphrase support.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use it as the label-free proxy for Recall@k. For gold evidence passages use Recall@k directly.

source.cite: Ragas v0.4.3 source code and docs (not in the RAGAS paper)
source.where: src/ragas/metrics/_context_recall.py, ContextRecallClassificationPrompt (instruction: 'analyze each sentence in the answer and classify if the sentence can be attributed to the given context') and LLMContextRecall._compute_score lines 114-123: sum(attributed)/len(classifications), NaN if none; docs context_recall.md

units.name: Context entity recall (RAGAS)
units.question: Does the retrieved context mention the key entities of the reference answer?
units.symbols: RE = set of entities in the reference answer; CE = set of entities in the retrieved context.

inputs.other: an entity extractor (an LLM in Ragas; any NER or a concept list works)

worked_example.setup: RE = {gradient descent, learning rate, SGD, momentum}. CE = {gradient descent, learning rate, momentum, batch size}.
worked_example.steps: Overlap = {gradient descent, learning rate, momentum} = 3. CER = 3/4.

units.blind_spots: Entity matching is string-fragile (SGD vs stochastic gradient descent). Mentions are not understanding. Good for entity-heavy QA, weak for explanations.
units.use_vs_neighbours: In a concept-graph tutor, the entity list can come straight from the KG node ids, which makes this cheap and exact.

source.cite: Ragas v0.4.3 source code
source.where: src/ragas/metrics/_context_entities_recall.py: class docstring 'Context Entity recall = | CN intersect GN | / | GN |' and ContextEntityRecall._compute_score lines 125-131: len(set(context_entities) & set(ground_truth_entities)) / (len(ground_truth_entities) + 1e-8); entities extracted by an LLM prompt, contexts joined with newlines

units.name: Context relevance (RAGAS paper / TruLens)
units.question: How much of the retrieved context is actually needed to answer the question?
units.formula_latex: \mathrm{CR}=\frac{\text{number of sentences extracted as necessary}}{\text{total number of sentences in }c(q)}
units.symbols: c(q) = retrieved context for question q; the LLM extracts the sentences that are crucial to answer q. TruLens instead scores each chunk 0 to 1 and averages.

worked_example.setup: A context has 12 sentences. The judge extracts 3 as necessary.

units.blind_spots: Penalises useful background and redundancy equally. Hard to separate from judge verbosity. In the RAGAS paper, human agreement on context relevance was the weakest of the three dimensions (stated in the paper's WikiEval section; exact value not re-read).
units.use_vs_neighbours: This is the 'context relevance' leg of the TruLens RAG triad and of ARES. Use it to tune chunk size and top-k; use Precision@k when labels exist.

source.cite: Es, James, Espinosa-Anke, Schockaert 2024, RAGAS (verified: formula CR = extracted sentences / total sentences)

units.name: ARES score with prediction-powered inference
units.question: What is the estimated rate of context-relevant (or faithful, or relevant-answer) outputs, with a confidence interval, using few human labels?
units.symbols: f = a fine-tuned LM judge giving 0/1 for one dimension (context relevance, answer faithfulness or answer relevance); N unlabelled examples; n human-labelled examples with labels y; Delta_j = f(x_j) - y_j; sigma^2 = sample variances.

inputs.other: synthetic training data generated by an LLM

worked_example.setup: The judge says 'relevant' for 70% of 1,000 unlabelled outputs. On 100 human-labelled outputs it says 72% but humans say 68%.

units.blind_spots: Needs fine-tuning three classifiers and a labelled validation set. Intervals are only valid if the labelled and unlabelled sets come from the same distribution. Scores are for system ranking, not per-answer decisions.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use it when you can afford 100 to 300 human labels and want an honest interval for an automatic judge. RAGAS gives a number without an interval.

source.cite: Saad-Falcon, Khattab, Potts, Zaharia 2024, ARES (NAACL); verified that ARES uses prediction-powered inference with a small human-annotated set

units.name: Faithfulness / groundedness (RAGAS)
units.question: Is every claim in the answer supported by the retrieved context?
units.symbols: S = statements the LLM extracts from the answer; V = the subset the LLM judges as inferable from the retrieved context.

inputs.llm_judge: yes (statement extraction + verification); no gold answer needed

worked_example.setup: An answer has 5 statements. The judge finds 4 supported by the context.

units.blind_spots: Checks the answer against the context, not against the truth: a faithful answer to a wrong passage scores 1. Judge errors on paraphrase and on multi-step inference. Very short or evasive answers score high ('I do not know' is trivially faithful). In the LEA course tutor study faithfulness fell from 0.69 to 0.50 as the course drifted from the tuning course (reported in [[Agentic RAG in Education]]; abstract-level).
units.use_vs_neighbours: The core RAG hallucination check. Pair with answer correctness (is it true?) and answer relevancy (is it on topic?). The claim-level cousin is FActScore (checks against a knowledge source, not the retrieved context).

source.cite: Es, James, Espinosa-Anke, Schockaert 2024, RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation (EACL demo)

units.name: Answer relevancy (RAGAS)
units.question: Does the answer address the question that was asked?
units.symbols: q = the original question; q-hat_i = n questions an LLM generates from the answer alone (the RAGAS paper does not fix n; the Ragas library default, strictness, is 3); E = an embedding model (the paper uses text-embedding-ada-002); cos = cosine similarity. The Ragas library sets the score to 0 when every generated question is flagged noncommittal (answer = refusal or evasion).
units.range: 0 to 1 (cosine can be negative in theory)

worked_example.setup: Embeddings reduced to 2-D unit vectors. q = (1, 0). Three questions generated from the answer have cosines 0.9, 0.8, 0.6 with q.

units.blind_spots: Does not check truth: a confident wrong answer on topic scores high. Restating the question also scores high. Depends on the embedding model.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use with faithfulness: faithfulness asks 'is it supported?', answer relevancy asks 'is it on topic?'. The two together catch the evasive and the off-topic answer.

source.cite: Es, James, Espinosa-Anke, Schockaert 2024, RAGAS (EACL demo), Eq. (1); library: Ragas ResponseRelevancy
source.where: paper Section 3 'Answer relevance', Eq. (1), PDF p.3; library src/ragas/metrics/_answer_relevance.py (strictness=3, noncommittal rule) at explodinggradients/ragas main @ 298b6827 (2026-02-23)

superseded.text: q = the original question; q-hat_i = N questions an LLM generates from the answer alone (N = 3 in the paper); E = an embedding model; cos = cosine similarity.

units.name: Answer correctness (RAGAS)
units.question: How close is the answer to the reference answer, in facts and in meaning?
units.symbols: TP = claims in both answer and reference; FP = claims only in the answer; FN = claims only in the reference; a, a* = answer and reference; defaults w_f = 0.75, w_s = 0.25 (Ragas docs).

worked_example.setup: Claims: 3 shared, 1 extra, 2 missing. Embedding cosine between answer and reference = 0.9.

units.blind_spots: The 0.75/0.25 weights are a default, not a theory. Needs a good reference. The semantic part rewards fluent near-misses.
units.use_vs_neighbours: The end-to-end 'is it right?' number for open answers. For short factual answers use EM / token F1, which are cheaper and exact.

source.cite: Ragas library source code (AnswerCorrectness, fbeta_score, AnswerSimilarity); not in the RAGAS paper

units.name: Exact match (EM)
units.question: Is the predicted answer string identical to a gold answer after normalisation?
units.symbols: norm = lowercase, remove punctuation and articles (a, an, the), collapse spaces; a-hat = prediction; a* = gold answers.

inputs.gold_labels: yes (one or more short gold answers)

worked_example.setup: Prediction 'The Gradient Descent.' vs gold 'gradient descent'.
worked_example.steps: Both normalise to 'gradient descent', so EM = 1. 'stochastic gradient descent' would give 0.

units.blind_spots: All-or-nothing; punishes correct paraphrase and longer correct answers. Useless for explanations. Models answer in sentences, so containment variants (gold string inside the output) are often used instead (RGB does this).
units.use_vs_neighbours: Short factoid and multi-hop QA (HotpotQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue). Add token F1 for partial credit.

units.name: Token F1
units.question: How much word overlap is there between the predicted and the gold answer?
units.formula_latex: P=\frac{|\hat a\cap a^*|}{|\hat a|},\ R=\frac{|\hat a\cap a^*|}{|a^*|},\ F_1=\frac{2PR}{P+R}
units.symbols: a-hat, a* = multisets of normalised tokens of the prediction and the gold answer; the intersection counts each token up to its minimum count. With several gold answers the question's score is the maximum F1 over the gold answers (SQuAD), then the average over questions (macro).

worked_example.setup: Prediction 'stochastic gradient descent method' (4 tokens); gold 'gradient descent' (2 tokens).

units.blind_spots: Bag of words: ignores order and meaning. 'not true' vs 'true' overlaps. Rewards verbose answers on recall.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Standard companion to EM for extractive QA. Not for long answers.

source.cite: Rajpurkar et al. 2016, SQuAD (EMNLP), Evaluation; official v1.1 evaluation script
source.where: paper Section 6.2 '(Macro-averaged) F1 score', PDF p.7; script f1_score() with Counter intersection and metric_max_over_ground_truths()

superseded.text: a-hat, a* = multisets of normalised tokens of the prediction and the gold answer; the intersection counts each token up to its minimum count.

units.name: ROUGE-L
units.question: How long is the longest shared word sequence between the answer and the reference?
units.symbols: X = reference tokens, Y = candidate tokens; LCS = length of the longest common subsequence (words in order, gaps allowed); beta = 1 gives balanced F.

worked_example.setup: Reference 'the cat sat on the mat' (6 words); candidate 'the cat on the mat' (5 words).
worked_example.steps: LCS = 5 (the cat on the mat). R = 5/6, P = 5/5 = 1. F = 2 x 1 x 0.833 / 1.833.

units.blind_spots: Surface overlap only. Weakly correlated with correctness for long-form answers (ALCE cites this for ELI5). A fluent wrong answer sharing words scores well.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Used by GraphRAG-Bench-style generation scoring as a cheap lexical score. Treat as a sanity metric, never the headline.

source.cite: Lin 2004, ROUGE: A Package for Automatic Evaluation of Summaries (ACL Workshop on Text Summarization Branches Out)
source.where: Section 3.1 'Sentence-Level LCS', Eqs. (2)-(4), PDF p.2

units.name: BLEU
units.question: How many n-grams of the answer appear in the reference, with a penalty for being too short?
units.symbols: p_n = clipped n-gram precision (candidate n-grams counted at most as often as in the reference); w_n = 1/N; c = candidate length; r = effective reference length (the length of the reference closest in length to the candidate; summed over the corpus). In the paper p_n and BP are corpus-level, the baseline is N = 4 with w_n = 1/N, and the score is 0 if any p_n = 0 (log 0).

worked_example.setup: Candidate 'the cat is on the mat' (6 words), reference 'there is a cat on the mat' (7 words), N = 2.
worked_example.steps: p1 = 5/6: the reference has 'the' once, so the candidate's second 'the' is clipped; matches are the, cat, is, on, mat = 5 of 6. p2 = 2/5 (on the, the mat). BP = exp(1 - 7/6) = 0.8465. BLEU-2 = 0.8465 x sqrt(5/6 x 2/5).

units.blind_spots: Precision only (the brevity penalty is a patch). Zero if any n-gram order has no match (needs smoothing at sentence level). Poor for open answers.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Machine translation heritage. Include only to compare with older papers; prefer BERTScore or judge metrics for open answers.

source.cite: Papineni, Roukos, Ward, Zhu 2002, BLEU: a Method for Automatic Evaluation of Machine Translation (ACL)
source.where: Section 2.2.1-2.3 (modified n-gram precision, brevity penalty, BLEU = BP exp(sum w_n log p_n)), PDF p.4-5

superseded.text: p_n = clipped n-gram precision (candidate n-grams counted at most as often as in the reference); w_n = 1/N; c = candidate length; r = reference length.

units.name: BERTScore
units.question: Does each word of the answer have a semantically close word in the reference, and the other way round?
units.formula_latex: R_{BERT}=\frac1{|x|}\sum_{x_i\in x}\max_{\hat x_j\in\hat x}x_i^{\top}\hat x_j,\quad P_{BERT}=\frac1{|\hat x|}\sum_{\hat x_j}\max_{x_i}x_i^{\top}\hat x_j,\quad F_{BERT}=\frac{2PR}{P+R}
units.symbols: x = reference token embeddings, x-hat = candidate token embeddings (contextual, from a BERT-like model, unit length so the dot product is the cosine).

inputs.other: a pretrained encoder

worked_example.setup: Toy 2-D unit vectors. Reference tokens: (1,0), (0,1), (0.707,0.707). Candidate tokens: (0.9,0.436), (0.2,0.98) after normalising.
worked_example.steps: Each reference token takes its best candidate cosine: R = mean of the three maxima. Each candidate token takes its best reference cosine: P = mean of two maxima. F = 2PR/(P+R).

units.blind_spots: Raw scores sit in a narrow high band (0.8 to 0.95), so differences look small; use baseline rescaling. Depends on the encoder and language. Still blind to factual errors that keep the topic.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Better than ROUGE/BLEU for paraphrase. Use when you have a reference but not a judge budget. Not a substitute for faithfulness.

source.cite: Zhang, Kishore, Wu, Weinberger, Artzi 2020, BERTScore: Evaluating Text Generation with BERT (ICLR)
source.where: Section 3 'BERTScore', R_BERT, P_BERT, F_BERT equations, PDF p.4 (read from the rendered page; text layer has no equations)

units.name: Embedding semantic similarity
units.question: Are the answer and the reference close in meaning, as seen by an embedding model?
units.symbols: E = a sentence embedding model.

inputs.other: an embedding model

units.range: -1 to 1 (the practical range depends on the embedding model)

worked_example.steps: Dot product = 0.48 + 0.48 = 0.96; both have length 1. cos = 0.96.

units.blind_spots: Topic similarity, not truth: 'Adam converges' and 'Adam does not converge' are close. Scores depend on the model; thresholds do not transfer.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Cheap and fast; use as a soft check next to EM / F1 or inside answer correctness. Never alone.

units.name: Citation recall (ALCE)
units.question: Is every statement in the answer fully supported by the passages it cites?
units.symbols: S = statements of the answer; C_s = passages cited for s; phi = NLI model (TRUE) returning 1 if the concatenated citations entail s.

inputs.llm_judge: yes (NLI entailment model); no gold answer

worked_example.setup: 3 statements. s1 cites [1][2] and is entailed; s2 cites [3] and is not; s3 cites [2][4][5] and is entailed.

units.blind_spots: Only entailment by the cited text, not truth of the passage. NLI models miss multi-sentence reasoning. An uncited statement counts as unsupported, which pressures models to over-cite.
units.use_vs_neighbours: The citation-quality leg for a tutor that must point at textbook pages. Pair with citation precision, because spraying citations raises recall.

source.cite: Gao, Yen, Yu, Chen 2023, Enabling LLMs to Generate Text with Citations (ALCE), EMNLP

units.name: Citation precision (ALCE)
units.question: Does each citation actually help, or are some irrelevant?
units.formula_latex: \mathrm{CitPrec}=\frac{\sum_{s}\#\{\text{citations of }s\text{ that are not irrelevant}\}}{\sum_{s}|C_s|},\ \ c_i\text{ irrelevant}\iff\phi(c_i,s)=0\ \wedge\ \phi(C_s\setminus c_i,s)=1
units.symbols: A citation c_i for statement s is irrelevant if it alone does not entail s and removing it does not hurt the other citations jointly entailing s. If the set does not entail s at all (recall 0), all its citations count as not precise (ALCE figure).

worked_example.setup: As above: s1 [1][2] both useful (2 ok of 2). s2 [3] not entailed (0 ok of 1). s3 [2][4][5]: [2] irrelevant (2 ok of 3).
worked_example.steps: CitPrec = (2 + 0 + 2) / (2 + 1 + 3) = 4/6. This matches the 4/6 = 66% of the ALCE figure.

units.blind_spots: Leave-one-out logic makes it unstable with redundant citations. Rewards under-citing (one citation, entailed). Needs the NLI judge to be right about entailment.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Always report with citation recall. For a tutor, add a page-level hit check (does the cited page contain the gold evidence?) as a cheap exact check.

source.cite: Gao et al. 2023 (ALCE)
source.id: arXiv:2305.14627 (the 4/6 example is in the paper figure 3)

units.name: FActScore (atomic fact precision)
units.question: What share of the atomic facts in a long answer is supported by a trusted knowledge source?
units.formula_latex: \mathrm{FActScore}=\frac1{|\mathcal Y|}\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y}\mathbb{1}\big[y\ \text{supported by knowledge source }\mathcal C\big]
units.symbols: Y = atomic facts extracted from the generation; C = knowledge source (for us: the course textbook chunks, not Wikipedia).

inputs.other: the knowledge source

worked_example.setup: A long answer breaks into 10 atomic facts; 7 are supported by the textbook.

units.blind_spots: Depends on the knowledge source covering the facts (true facts missing from the source count as errors). Does not penalise omissions. Atomic-fact splitting is itself an LLM step.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Like faithfulness but against a fixed source rather than the retrieved context, so it also catches retrieval misses. Useful for the plain-LLM arm, which has no retrieved context to be faithful to.

source.cite: Min et al. 2023, FActScore (EMNLP), Section 3.1 Definition; official package factscore
source.where: paper Section 3.1, PDF p.3: f(y) = (1/|A_y|) sum_{a in A_y} 1[a supported by C]; FActScore(M) = E_x[f(M_x) | M_x responds]; code factscore/factscorer.py get_score() (gamma=10 length penalty, init_score)

units.name: Hallucination rate
units.question: How often does the system say something unsupported or false?
units.symbols: N = answers; S, V as in faithfulness. State whether 'unsupported' is against the context (faithfulness view) or against a source of truth (factuality view).

worked_example.setup: 20 answers; 3 contain at least one unsupported claim.

units.blind_spots: Not one standard: definitions differ between papers, so numbers are not comparable. Response-level hides how many claims were wrong; claim-level hides that one wrong claim can ruin an answer.
units.use_vs_neighbours: The headline safety number for a tutor. Always give both levels and the definition. Use FActScore for fine-grained factuality.

source.cite: RAGAS (Es et al. 2024) Section 3, faithfulness F = |V|/|S|; SelfCheckGPT (Manakul et al. 2023)
source.where: RAGAS PDF p.3 (faithfulness); SelfCheckGPT Table 2 (AUC-PR, correlation): no hallucination-rate formula

units.name: Noise robustness (RGB)
units.question: Does accuracy hold up when some retrieved documents are irrelevant noise?
units.formula_latex: \mathrm{Acc}(r)=\frac1N\sum_{q}\mathbb{1}\big[a^*_q\subseteq\mathrm{response}_q\big]\ \ \text{with a fraction }r\text{ of the context replaced by noise}
units.symbols: r = noise ratio (RGB uses 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 over a fixed context size); a*_q = gold answer string; accuracy = the gold string appears in the response.

inputs.other: a pool of negative (noise) documents per question

worked_example.setup: RGB Table (English, ChatGPT, read in the paper): accuracy 96.33 at noise ratio 0, 90.00 at 0.6, 76.00 at 0.8.

units.blind_spots: String containment can credit a response that lists many candidates. Noise from the same topic is harder than random noise; RGB's noise is topical but not answer-bearing.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Answers 'is the generator distracted by wrong context?'. Matters for vector RAG with a noisy top-k and for GraphRAG subgraphs full of neighbours.

source.cite: Chen, Lin, Han, Sun 2024, Benchmarking Large Language Models in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RGB), AAAI

units.name: Negative rejection (RGB)
units.question: When the context has no answer, does the system say so instead of guessing?
units.symbols: N_neg = questions whose context contains only negative (non-answer) documents; rejection phrase = a fixed 'insufficient information' string the prompt tells the model to output.

inputs.gold_labels: questions with no answer in the context

worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 50 questions with only noise documents; the model says 'insufficient information' in 11.

units.blind_spots: A model that always refuses scores 1.0: pair with accuracy on answerable questions. The phrase test depends on following the prompt format.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Key for a tutor: out-of-scope questions must not get an invented answer. Our question bank has an out-of-scope type for exactly this.

units.name: Information integration (RGB)
units.question: Can the system combine facts from several passages into one correct answer?
units.symbols: Q_int = questions whose answer needs two or more documents.

worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 40 multi-document questions, 22 answered correctly.

units.blind_spots: Accuracy only; does not say which fact was missed. Easy to confuse with retrieval recall: a miss may be retrieval or reasoning.
units.use_vs_neighbours: A cheap multi-hop check before the heavier HotpotQA-style joint metrics. Compare vector RAG and GraphRAG on this slice.

units.name: Counterfactual robustness (RGB)
units.question: If the context contains a factual error, does the system notice it and still give the right answer?
units.formula_latex: \mathrm{ED}=\frac{\#\text{ errors flagged}}{N_{\mathrm{cf}}},\qquad \mathrm{EC}=\frac{\#\text{ correct answers after flagging}}{N_{\mathrm{cf}}}
units.symbols: N_cf = questions where the model knows the answer but the given documents state a wrong one; flagged = the response says the document is wrong. (Exact denominator of EC is as written in RGB for the 'after identifying' set; check the paper before reuse.)

inputs.other: documents with deliberately wrong facts

worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 50 counterfactual questions. The model flags the error in 12 and gives the correct answer in 5 of those.
worked_example.steps: ED = 12/50 = 0.24. EC = 5/50 = 0.10 on this denominator (or 5/12 = 0.417 if defined over flagged cases).

units.blind_spots: Conflicts with the common wish that a RAG system trust its context. For a course tutor the textbook is the authority, so low ED is expected and desired unless the textbook is wrong.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use only if your corpus can be wrong (web pages). For a curated textbook, report it as a stress test, not a target.

units.name: LLM-as-judge pairwise win rate
units.question: In head-to-head comparisons, how often does a judge prefer system A over system B?
units.symbols: W = comparisons the judge prefers A; T = ties; L = A loses; N = number of (question, run) pairs. Run each pair in both orders and keep only order-consistent verdicts (or count inconsistent ones as ties).

inputs.llm_judge: yes (a strong LLM, different from the answer model)

worked_example.setup: 10 judged pairs: A wins 6, ties 2, loses 2.

units.blind_spots: Judge biases: position, verbosity (longer wins), self-preference (a judge prefers its own family). A win rate says who is better, not by how much or whether either is correct. Needs significance testing.
units.use_vs_neighbours: The right tool when there is no gold answer (global summaries, explanations). Use correctness metrics when gold exists. Validate the judge against humans (Cohen's kappa).

source.cite: AlpacaEval (tatsu-lab/alpaca_eval) win-rate code for the tie-as-half convention; Zheng et al. 2023 (MT-Bench) Section 3.4 for the swap protocol
source.where: src/alpaca_eval/metrics/winrate.py get_winrate and metrics/helpers.py ScoringRule.describe_head2head (draw encoded 1.5, win_rate = mean(preference - 1)); MT-Bench PDF p.6 'Swapping positions': declare a win only when preferred in both orders, else tie

units.name: Judge position consistency
units.question: Does the judge give the same verdict when the two answers swap places?
units.formula_latex: \mathrm{Cons}=\frac{\#\{\text{pairs with the same winner in both orders}\}}{N},\qquad \mathrm{FirstPref}=\frac{\#\{\text{times the first slot wins}\}}{2N}
units.symbols: Each pair is judged twice (A,B) and (B,A). Cons = share with the same underlying winner; FirstPref = share of all verdicts where the first-listed answer won (0.5 = no position bias).

worked_example.setup: 50 pairs judged in both orders (100 verdicts). The same winner in 38 pairs. The first-listed answer wins 55 of the 100 verdicts.
worked_example.steps: Cons = 38/50 = 0.76. FirstPref = 55/100 = 0.55 (0.5 would be no position bias).

units.blind_spots: Consistency can be high for a judge that is consistently wrong. Does not measure verbosity or self-preference bias.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Report it for any judge-based result; it is the cheapest judge health check. Zheng et al. found position bias in the judges they tested (reported in the paper).

source.cite: Zheng et al. 2023 (MT-Bench) Table 2; Wang et al. 2023, Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators (Conflict Rate)
source.where: MT-Bench PDF p.5 Table 2 (Consistency, Biased toward first/second); Wang et al. PDF p.3 (Conflict Rate = share of conflicting results over both orders)

units.name: Joint answer + citation correctness (course handout)
units.question: Is the answer right AND does it cite every gold document, so the right answer is not a lucky guess?
units.formula_latex: P=\frac{|C\cap G|}{|C|}\ (\text{1 if }C=\emptyset\text{ and the system abstained}),\quad R=\frac{|C\cap G|}{|G|},\quad F_1=\frac{2PR}{P+R},\quad \mathrm{Joint}=\mathbb{1}[\mathrm{EM}=1\ \wedge\ C\supseteq G]
units.symbols: C = set of document ids the answer cites; G = gold supporting documents; EM = exact match after normalisation. Joint is 1 only if the answer is exactly right and the citations cover all gold documents (extra citations are allowed here, so precision is reported separately).

inputs.gold_labels: gold answer and gold supporting documents
inputs.other: the cited document ids from the structured answer

worked_example.setup: 6 questions. EM = [1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0]. Gold sets and cited sets: q1 G={d1,d2} C={d1,d2}; q2 G={d1,d2} C={d1}; q3 G={d3} C={d3,d9}; q4 G={d4} C={d4} (but EM=0); q5 G={d5,d6} C={d5,d6,d8}; q6 G={d7} C={} (EM=0).
worked_example.steps: Joint per question = EM and C superset of G: [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0]. Mean = 3/6.

units.blind_spots: Superset test rewards over-citing (q3, q5 pass with a wrong extra citation), so always report citation precision beside it. Multi-hop answers can be right with a partial gold set (an alternative valid path), which Joint marks as a failure. Needs gold supporting documents, which most open-domain sets lack.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use it where gold evidence documents exist (2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, MuSiQue). It is the document-level cousin of HotpotQA joint F1 (joint_f1); ALCE citation precision/recall judge support with an NLI model instead of gold ids.

source.cite: Course handout (IUST Advanced NLP RAG/GraphRAG project), student_handout.pdf section 2.8; compare Yang et al. 2018 (HotpotQA) joint metric

units.notes: Formula read in the handout (P, R, F1 and Joint = I[EM=1 and C superset G]). Document-level, no LLM judge.

units.name: Counterfactual abstention, hallucination and lucky-correct rates
units.question: When the gold documents are hidden, does the system say 'I do not know', make something up, or get the answer right by luck?
units.symbols: a = the system's abstain flag; EM = exact match of its answer; each rate is the mean over the masked question subset. The three rates are a partition and sum to 1.

inputs.gold_labels: questions whose gold documents are masked from retrieval
inputs.other: abstain flag and EM per question; masked-evidence run (allow_doc predicate)

units.higher_is_better: abstention higher, hallucination lower; lucky-correct is a contamination signal (lower is better)

worked_example.setup: 10 masked questions (gold documents hidden). Abstain flags: 4 abstain. Among the 6 that answer: 2 are exactly right (lucky), 4 are wrong. (illustrative)

units.blind_spots: Abstention is not the same as 'unanswerable': other passages or pretraining knowledge can still support the answer, so the handout subset keeps only questions whose answer string appears in no non-gold paragraph, and still reports lucky-correct. A parse failure must not count as abstention (it is a format error), otherwise hallucination is understated. The test measures behaviour when evidence is hidden, not when it is merely weak.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Closer to RGB negative rejection (negative_rejection) than to a plain hallucination_rate: it masks gold evidence instead of supplying noise passages, and it separates 'wrong' from 'right by luck'. Use MuSiQue-Full unanswerable contrast questions for a label-based version.

source.cite: Course handout (IUST Advanced NLP), student_handout.pdf section 2.8 and 4.5 (Counterfactual subset: 50 val and 100 test questions)

units.notes: Definitions read in the handout; the example numbers are invented for teaching.

units.name: Accuracy by gold-passage position (Lost in the Middle)
units.question: Does the answer get worse when the relevant passage sits in the middle of a long context?
units.formula_latex: \mathrm{Acc}(p)=\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q\in Q}\mathbb{1}\big[\text{a gold answer string appears in the model output for }q\text{ with the gold passage at position }p\big],\qquad \text{gap}=\max_p\mathrm{Acc}(p)-\min_p\mathrm{Acc}(p)
units.symbols: p = position of the gold passage among N passages (1 = first); Q = questions; the other N-1 passages are distractors in fixed order. Plot Acc(p) against p. Correct = any gold answer string appears in the output (Liu et al. 2023, Section 2), not strict exact match.

inputs.gold_labels: questions with one known gold passage
inputs.other: the ability to place the gold passage at chosen positions

worked_example.setup: 20 passages in context. Accuracy with the gold passage at positions 1, 5, 10, 15, 20: {1: 0.78, 5: 0.62, 10: 0.55, 15: 0.6, 20: 0.74}. (illustrative shape, invented numbers)

units.blind_spots: A property of the model and context length, not of retrieval; the U-shape depends on model, context size and prompt. Needs a controlled experiment (same questions, only the order changes). With few questions each point has a wide interval (use bootstrap_ci).
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use it to choose the context order (best passages first and last) and to explain why a higher recall@k can still lower the answer score. Not a retrieval metric (recall_at_k) and not a faithfulness metric.

source.cite: Liu et al. 2023, Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (TACL 2024)
source.where: Section 2 'Multi-Document Question Answering', 2.1 Experimental Setup, PDF p.2-3 (accuracy = any correct answer appears in the predicted output; distractors from Contriever in decreasing relevance; best- vs worst-case difference)

units.notes: Only the experiment design is taken from the paper; its numbers were not re-read for this run. The curve here is invented.

superseded.text: \mathrm{Acc}(p)=\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q\in Q}\mathrm{EM}\big(q,\ \text{context with the gold passage at position }p\big),\qquad \text{gap}=\max_p\mathrm{Acc}(p)-\min_p\mathrm{Acc}(p)
p = position of the gold passage among N passages (1 = first); Q = questions; the other N-1 passages are distractors in fixed order. Plot Acc(p) against p.

units.name: Abstention accuracy and over-abstention
units.question: Across answerable and unanswerable questions, does the system abstain exactly when it should?
units.symbols: TP = unanswerable and abstained; FN = unanswerable but answered; FP = answerable but abstained; TN = answerable and answered; N = all questions.

inputs.other: abstain flag

units.higher_is_better: AbsAcc and AbsRecall higher; OverAbs lower

worked_example.setup: N=100 questions: 24 unanswerable (18 abstained, 6 answered) and 76 answerable (9 wrongly abstained, 67 answered). (illustrative)
worked_example.steps: AbsAcc = (18+67)/100 = 0.85; AbsRecall = 18/24 = 0.750 (this is RGB negative rejection); OverAbs = 9/76 = 0.118.

units.blind_spots: A system that always abstains has AbsRecall 1.0 and OverAbs 1.0, so never report one number alone. 'Unanswerable' labels are design-dependent (MuSiQue-Full builds them by removing a supporting paragraph; hiding gold documents in a corpus with other support is weaker). Say how the abstain flag is detected (JSON flag vs refusal phrase).
units.use_vs_neighbours: Extends negative_rejection (recall only) with the cost of refusing answerable questions; counterfactual_abstention_triplet is the masked-evidence version without answerable controls. Compare with hallucination_rate on the answered subset.

units.name: Judge length bias (length-exploitation check)
units.question: Does the judge, or the model being tuned, win just by writing longer answers?
units.symbols: w_i = 1 if the candidate wins pair i; Δlen_i = length(candidate) - length(baseline) in tokens; M = pairs whose lengths differ by at most a tolerance epsilon. Report mean length of both systems too.

inputs.other: token lengths of both responses

units.range: correlation -1 to 1; matched win rate 0 to 1
units.higher_is_better: correlation near 0 and matched win rate close to the raw win rate

worked_example.steps: Pearson correlation of length difference and win = 0.75. Matched pairs (|diff| <= 20): 3 pairs, wins 2 of 3 -> matched win rate = 0.67.

units.blind_spots: Matching on length throws away data and 10 pairs are far too few (the example is only arithmetic). Length can legitimately correlate with quality (completeness). A regression-based length-controlled win rate (AlpacaEval) is better than a hard tolerance but needs more pairs.

units.name: Comprehensiveness (win rate)
units.question: Does the answer cover all aspects and details of the question?
units.symbols: c = criterion (How much detail does the answer provide to cover all aspects and details of the question); Q = 125 sensemaking questions; R = 5 repeated judgements; the judge sees both answers and the criterion definition. The 'tie' rule is an assumption (unverified in the paper text).

inputs.other: questions without gold answers (generated from persona / task prompts)

worked_example.setup: Illustrative judge outcomes for 125 questions x 5 repeats = 625 verdicts of GraphRAG (A) vs vector RAG (B): A preferred 400, B preferred 200, no preference 25 (ties counted 0.5).

units.blind_spots: Longer answers tend to win (verbosity bias). Rewards coverage, not correctness. Judge is an LLM, so the usual judge biases apply. Edge et al. report GraphRAG global approaches at 72 to 83% on podcast data and 72 to 80% on news against vector RAG (paper text).
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use for global, corpus-wide questions where coverage matters. Not for single facts, where vector RAG is better and shorter.
