units.name: Supporting-fact F1 (HotpotQA)
units.question: Did the system point to the right supporting sentences, not just the right answer?
units.formula_latex: P_{sp}=\frac{|\hat S\cap S^*|}{|\hat S|},\ R_{sp}=\frac{|\hat S\cap S^*|}{|S^*|},\ F1_{sp}=\frac{2P_{sp}R_{sp}}{P_{sp}+R_{sp}}
units.symbols: S* = gold supporting facts (document title, sentence index); S-hat = predicted supporting facts.

worked_example.setup: Gold facts {(A,0), (B,2)}. Predicted {(A,0), (B,1), (C,0)}.

units.blind_spots: Needs gold evidence labels, which our own bank must supply. A system can have the right answer by luck or by memory and get this wrong (and the reverse).
units.use_vs_neighbours: The explainability check for multi-hop questions; for our tutor, replace sentence ids with textbook page / chunk ids.

source.cite: Yang et al. 2018, HotpotQA (EMNLP)
source.where: Experiments, metrics paragraph (p.7, EM and F1 on the set of supporting-fact sentences); formula read in official eval code: update_sp() in hotpot_evaluate_v1.py in github.com/hotpotqa/hotpot, master, last commit fa3a363 (2018-10-05)

units.name: Joint answer + evidence F1 (HotpotQA)
units.question: Is the answer right and is the evidence right, both at once?
units.symbols: P_ans, R_ans = token precision and recall of the answer; P_sp, R_sp as in supporting-fact F1. (The joint EM variant requires both EM scores to be 1.)

worked_example.setup: Answer: P = 1, R = 0.5. Evidence: P = 1/3, R = 1/2 (from the previous example).

units.blind_spots: Harsh: multiplying makes it hard to score above 0.5. Rewards exact evidence match, which a different but valid evidence set fails.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use when you want one multi-hop number that cannot be gamed by guessing answers. Report answer F1 and evidence F1 separately too.

source.cite: Yang et al. 2018, HotpotQA (EMNLP)
source.where: Experiments, metrics paragraph (p.7) printed equations for P(joint) = P(ans)P(sup), R(joint) = R(ans)R(sup), Joint F1 = 2PR/(P+R); joint EM = 1 only if both EM are 1; confirmed in joint_f1/joint_em of hotpot_evaluate_v1.py in github.com/hotpotqa/hotpot, master, last commit fa3a363 (2018-10-05)

units.name: All-hop (complete evidence) recall@k
units.question: For multi-hop questions, did retrieval bring back all the needed passages, not just one?
units.symbols: G_q = the set of gold supporting passages for question q (2 to 4 hops); Ret_q,k = top-k retrieved passages.

worked_example.setup: 4 questions. q1 needs {a,b}, both retrieved. q2 needs {a,b}, only a retrieved. q3 needs {c,d}, both retrieved. q4 needs {e}, retrieved.
worked_example.steps: Complete: q1, q3, q4 = 3 of 4 = 0.75. Per-passage recall would be 6/7 = 0.857, which hides the failed hop.

units.blind_spots: Strict; depends on k. Says nothing about answer quality. Requires annotated evidence for every hop.
units.use_vs_neighbours: The cleanest place for GraphRAG to show its value: graph traversal is meant to fetch the second hop that similarity search misses. Compare vector RAG and GraphRAG on this at equal k or equal token budget.

source.cite: Xiong et al. 2021, Multi-hop dense retrieval (ICLR) and Asai et al. 2020 (SP EM, as cited there); nearest named variant, 2-hop only
source.where: Sec. 3.1.2 'Reranking' and footnote 5 (p.4): Support Passage Exact Match = 'whether the final predicted sequence covers both gold passages'

superseded.text: Trivedi et al. 2022, MuSiQue (all supporting paragraphs); Ho et al. 2020, 2WikiMultiHopQA (evidence paths); metric name is common practice, not one paper

units.name: Triple precision / recall / F1
units.question: Of the (head, relation, tail) triples we extracted, how many are right, and how many of the right ones did we get?
units.symbols: T_pred = extracted triples after normalising names; T_gold = annotated triples for the same text. Matching can be exact, normalised, embedding-fuzzy or LLM-judged: say which.

worked_example.setup: 10 extracted triples, 7 appear in the gold set; the gold set has 12 triples.

units.blind_spots: Gold is never complete: valid extra triples count as errors. Matching rules swing the number by tens of points. Does not check whether the graph helps answers.
units.use_vs_neighbours: The first KG quality gate (pilot on about 200 gold triples as in the architecture plan). Use schema conformance for 'is it well-formed' and downstream QA metrics for 'is it useful'.

source.cite: Mihindukulasooriya et al. 2023, Text2KGBench
source.where: 'Evaluation Metrics' section, 'Fact Extraction Accuracy' (p.6-7): P = correct LLM triples / LLM triples, R = correct LLM triples / ground-truth triples, F1 harmonic mean

units.name: Entity-resolution pairwise F1
units.question: Did we merge the mentions that refer to the same concept, and only those?
units.symbols: C_pred, C_gold = clusterings of mentions into concepts; pairs(C) = all unordered mention pairs placed in the same cluster.

worked_example.setup: Mentions a..e. Gold clusters {a,b,c}, {d,e}. Predicted {a,b}, {c,d,e}.
worked_example.steps: Predicted pairs: ab, cd, ce, de = 4. Gold pairs: ab, ac, bc, de = 4. Correct: ab, de = 2. P = 2/4, R = 2/4, F1 = 0.5.

units.blind_spots: Quadratic in cluster size: one big wrong merge dominates. Does not show whether a merge loses a distinction that matters (e.g. 'bias' vs 'bias term').
units.use_vs_neighbours: Check after normalising 'SGD', 'stochastic gradient descent'. If the KG is built with fixed concept ids from an ontology (CSO) this reduces to alignment accuracy.

source.cite: Shearer 2024, Hands-On Entity Resolution (O'Reilly)
source.where: Ch. 11, 'Pairwise Approach' / 'Cluster-Based Approach' and Fig. 11-1 (printed p.174-175): predictions compared with a gold cluster view per record pair; Precision = TP/(TP+FP), Recall = TP/(TP+FN)

units.name: Schema / ontology conformance
units.question: Are the extracted triples well-formed according to our relation and type schema?
units.symbols: T = extracted triples; R = allowed relations; dom(r), rng(r) = allowed head and tail types of relation r.

inputs.other: the schema; no gold triples needed

worked_example.setup: 50 triples; 40 use an allowed relation with allowed head and tail types.

units.blind_spots: Well-formed is not true. A perfectly conformant graph can be wrong. A tight schema can force wrong labels.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Cheap, label-free, runs on every build. Use it as a regression test, and triple F1 for correctness.

source.cite: Mihindukulasooriya et al. 2023, Text2KGBench
source.where: 'Evaluation Metrics' section, 'Ontology Conformance' (p.7): OC = ontology-conforming LLM output triples / total LLM output triples; domain and range checks named as a possible extension

units.name: Prerequisite-edge precision / recall
units.question: Does the KG have the right 'X is a prerequisite of Y' edges, in the right direction?
units.formula_latex: P=\frac{|E_{pred}\cap E_{gold}|}{|E_{pred}|},\ R=\frac{|E_{pred}\cap E_{gold}|}{|E_{gold}|},\ \text{direction counts: }(u\to v)\neq(v\to u)
units.symbols: E = sets of directed prerequisite edges. Variants: compare transitive closures (a transitive edge is not an error) or reduced graphs.

inputs.gold_labels: yes (expert prerequisite pairs, e.g. LectureBank, MOOCCubeX)

worked_example.setup: Gold chain A to B to C to D. Predicted A to B, C to B (reversed), C to D, A to D (shortcut).
worked_example.steps: Correct directed edges: A to B, C to D = 2. P = 2/4 = 0.5, R = 2/3 = 0.667. Against the transitive closure A to D would also be right: P = 3/4.

units.blind_spots: Annotation disagreement on prerequisites is high. Direction errors and transitive shortcuts must be handled by a stated rule.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Specific to the tutor. It scores the structure that makes the graph arm different from the vector arm.

source.cite: Li et al. 2019, LectureBank / What should I learn first (AAAI)
source.where: Experiments (p.6): prerequisite chain learning treated as binary classification over concept pairs, reporting precision, recall and F1; edge direction A to B means A is a prerequisite of B

units.name: Evidence (subgraph) recall
units.question: Does the retrieved subgraph contain the triples that are needed to answer?
units.symbols: G* = gold evidence triples (or gold evidence nodes / edges) for question q; S_q = triples in the retrieved subgraph.

worked_example.setup: Gold evidence: 3 triples. The retrieved subgraph of 40 triples holds 2 of them.

units.blind_spots: A huge subgraph gets recall 1 trivially: always report subgraph size or precision with it. Needs evidence annotations.
units.use_vs_neighbours: The graph analogue of Recall@k. Use it to decide the hop depth and the node budget.

source.cite: Li et al. 2025, Simple Is Effective: SubgraphRAG (ICLR 2025)
source.where: 'Evaluation Metrics' (p.7) and Table 1: recall of shortest-path triples and of GPT-4o-identified relevant triples (up to 20) in the retrieved triples, computed per question then averaged

superseded.text: Common in KGQA / GraphRAG evaluation; see Peng et al. 2026, Graph RAG survey (Zotero VDYASD2W)

units.name: Subgraph precision (noise ratio)
units.question: How much of the retrieved subgraph is actually useful?
units.symbols: As above. For a token-based view: tokens of evidence triples / tokens of the whole serialised subgraph.

worked_example.setup: Same subgraph: 40 triples, 2 gold evidence triples retrieved.

units.blind_spots: Triples outside the gold set may still help a reader (context). A tiny subgraph with 100% precision may omit the answer.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Pairs with evidence recall like Precision pairs with Recall. High noise explains faithfulness drops (see noise robustness).

source.cite: Xiang et al. 2026, GraphRAG-Bench (ICLR 2026), nearest published analogue
source.where: Sec. 3.3 and App. F (p.25) Eq. 3: Context Relevance = mean over retrieved contexts of an LLM relevance judgement R(c, Q, E)

units.name: Answer-entity Hits@k
units.question: When the answer is a graph entity, is it in the top-k answers the system returns?
units.symbols: A*_q = gold answer entities; Top_k = the top-k answer entities.

worked_example.setup: 5 questions. The top-1 answer is correct for 3 of them.

units.blind_spots: Needs entity-level gold, not free text. Hits@1 punishes multi-answer questions.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use for path / link-style questions (TutorQA tasks: prerequisite prediction, path search). Not for free-form explanation answers.

source.cite: Luo et al. 2024, Reasoning on Graphs (ICLR); Mavromatis & Karypis 2024, GNN-RAG
source.where: RoG 'Evaluation Metrics' (p.7): Hits@1 = proportion of questions whose top-1 predicted answer is correct; GNN-RAG experiments (p.6): H@1 = accuracy of the first predicted answer, Hit = any true answer found in the generated response

units.name: Indexing cost and break-even queries
units.question: How many questions must the system answer before the expensive graph build pays for itself?
units.symbols: C_idx = one-off indexing cost (LLM tokens x price, plus time); c_q = mean cost per query; V = baseline (vector or full-text map-reduce), G = graph system; Q* = break-even number of queries.

inputs.other: token counts and prices from the run logs

worked_example.setup: Illustrative: graph index costs 30 USD, vector index 0.5 USD. For global questions, vector/map-reduce costs 0.50 USD per query, the graph root summaries 0.02 USD (Edge et al. report root-level community summaries need 9x to 43x fewer tokens, for example 26,657 vs 1,014,611 tokens for podcast data).

units.blind_spots: Prices change; the number is only valid for the stated model and prices. For local factual questions the graph is often not cheaper per query: then Q* is undefined.
units.use_vs_neighbours: A must-report for the thesis: graph indexing is the main cost (many LLM extraction calls). Report tokens, USD and wall time for indexing separately from per-query.

source.cite: Edge et al. 2024 (token counts: verified in the paper's context-token table); Xiao et al. 2025 GraphRAG-Bench reports indexing and retrieval efficiency

units.name: Triple groundedness rate (extraction hallucination proxy)
units.question: What share of the triples the LLM extracted are actually supported by the passage text?
units.symbols: T = triples extracted from a passage; the check is a string match after fixed normalisation (lower-case, NFKD, strip punctuation and articles, collapse spaces): the object must occur in the passage text or title, the subject must equal the title or occur in the text.

inputs.other: extracted triples and their source passages; no gold triples needed

worked_example.setup: One passage: 'Thomas Carr directed Alias Billy the Kid, released in 1946.' Title 'Alias Billy the Kid'. Extracted triples: (Alias Billy the Kid, director, Thomas Carr) ; (Alias Billy the Kid, publication date, 1946) ; (Alias Billy the Kid, country, United States).
worked_example.steps: Triple 1: object 'Thomas Carr' in text, subject = title -> grounded. Triple 2: '1946' in text -> grounded. Triple 3: 'United States' not in text -> ungrounded. Groundedness = 2/3.

units.blind_spots: It is a proxy for hallucination, not precision: a true fact that the passage implies but does not state (country inferred from context) counts as ungrounded, and a grounded string can still be the wrong relation or direction. String matching misses paraphrase. It needs no gold triples, so pair it with triple recall against gold (triple_prf, evidence_triple_recall).
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use it as a cheap filter during KG construction and as a hallucination proxy next to triple_prf (needs gold triples) and schema_conformance (checks relations against the vocabulary).

source.cite: IUST Advanced NLP course handout (student_handout.pdf), local; analogue: Text2KGBench subject/object hallucination
source.id: a local script (not published) (41 pp.); arXiv:2308.02357 v1
source.where: Handout p.27 (kg build: groundedness control, object in text or paragraph title, subject equal to the title or in the text, after fixed normalisation) and p.33 (kg eval: groundedness rate as a hallucination proxy; fixed normalisation = lower-case, NFKD, strip marks and articles, collapse spaces). Text2KGBench p.7: SH/OH check that subject/object occur in the sentence or ontology concepts, with stemming

units.notes: The handout describes groundedness in words as a hallucination proxy and gives the check rule; no formula was printed, so the ratio is our reading. The example is invented.

units.name: Latency per stage (and time to first token)
units.question: Where does the time go: retrieval, reranking, graph traversal, or generation?
units.formula_latex: T_{\mathrm{e2e}}=\sum_{s\in\text{stages}}T_s,\qquad \text{share}_s=\frac{T_s}{T_{\mathrm{e2e}}}\ \ (\text{percentiles of each stage reported separately; they do not add})
units.symbols: T_s = measured time of stage s for one query; TTFT = time until the first generated token.

inputs.other: trace spans per stage (the eval harness traces)

worked_example.setup: One query: embed + vector search 45 ms, rerank 120 ms, graph expansion 80 ms, generation 1800 ms.

units.blind_spots: p95 of the sum is not the sum of p95s. Streaming makes TTFT, not total time, what the student feels.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Decide where to optimise. For a tutor, TTFT and p95 matter more than the mean.

source.cite: Systems practice; no primary source found
source.where: Nothing to read: the entry is a definition (sum of stage times, share = T_s/T_e2e). The statement 'percentiles of the sum are not the sum of percentiles' is a standard property of percentiles, not sourced here; MLflow Tracing docs not opened.

units.name: Tokens and cost per answer
units.question: How many tokens and how much money does one answer cost?
units.symbols: t_in = prompt tokens including retrieved context; t_out = generated tokens; p_in, p_out = price per million input and output tokens. Add embedding and judge calls for a full cost.

inputs.other: token counts from the API usage field; the price table, dated

worked_example.setup: 6,500 input tokens, 400 output tokens, prices 0.25 and 2.00 USD per million (the gpt-5-mini row of [[Model Benchmarks - CS-ML QA and Text-to-Graph]], 2026-10-02).

units.blind_spots: Cheap models make cost look negligible and hide that the graph arm uses far more context. Prices change; date every table. Cached tokens are billed less.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Report with accuracy as cost-normalised accuracy (correct answers per USD) so arms with larger contexts do not look free.

source.cite: Provider pricing pages (OpenAI/AvalAI) not opened; formula is arithmetic
source.where: Not read: the formula c = (t_in*p_in + t_out*p_out)/1e6 is the standard per-million-token billing, but no provider page was read in this pass. The vault note 'Model Benchmarks - CS-ML QA and Text-to-Graph' lists gpt-5-mini 0.25/2.00 as AvalAI prices; the OpenAI pricing page is JS-rendered and returned 403, so it was not verified.

units.name: Cost-normalised accuracy
units.question: How much correctness do we buy per dollar?
units.symbols: Acc = correctness (EM, F1 or judged); mean cost per query from cost_per_answer.

inputs.other: costs

worked_example.setup: Vector RAG: accuracy 0.62 at 0.0024 USD per answer. GraphRAG: accuracy 0.68 at 0.0090 USD (illustrative).

units.blind_spots: A ratio hides absolute levels: a cheap wrong system can win. Show accuracy and cost side by side, then the ratio.
units.use_vs_neighbours: A tie-breaker for choosing between close arms. Plot accuracy versus cost (a Pareto chart) rather than only the ratio.

source.cite: Ours (derived); no primary source
source.where: Nothing to read: the metric is a ratio of two other metrics (accuracy / mean cost). No paper or library defines 'accuracy per dollar' in a standard way.

units.name: Throughput under concurrency (Little's law)
units.question: How many questions per second can the service handle with c students at once?
units.symbols: L = requests in the system (concurrency c); W = mean time per request in seconds; lambda = completed requests per second.

inputs.other: load test with fixed concurrency

worked_example.setup: 8 concurrent students, mean latency 2 s.
worked_example.steps: lambda_max = 8 / 2 s = 4 requests per second (if the provider does not rate-limit).

units.blind_spots: Rate limits and GPU batching break the linear model. Averages hide queueing at the tail.
units.use_vs_neighbours: For classroom size planning (30 students asking within a minute). Vector DB QPS is not the bottleneck: generation is.

source.cite: Little 2011, Little's Law as Viewed on its 50th Anniversary, Operations Research 59(3), 536-549 (restates Little 1961, Oper. Res. 9(3), 383-387)
source.where: Little 2011, Sec. 1 (p. 536): 'L = lambda W' - the average number of items in a queuing system equals the average arrival rate times the average time an item spends in the system (long-run, stationary); the original 1961 paper itself was behind a paywall (403) and was not read

units.name: Steps per query and failure-to-stop rate
units.question: For an agentic system, how many tool calls does it take, and how often does it never finish?
units.symbols: n_q = number of agent steps (tool calls) for query q; n_max = step cap.

inputs.other: agent trace

worked_example.setup: 20 queries with cap 8 steps: total 74 steps, 3 queries hit the cap.

units.blind_spots: Counts effort, not quality. A cap hides runaway loops that only cost money.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Only for the agentic arm. Report next to cost; see [[Agentic RAG in Education]] for the argument.

source.cite: Ours; no primary source
source.where: Nothing to read: mean steps and the share of queries that hit the step cap are our own counters. No paper opened to define 'failure-to-stop rate'.

units.name: Failure attribution rates (retrieval / rank-cutoff / generation)
units.question: For wrong answers, was the gold evidence never retrieved, retrieved but cut, or in context and still misused?
units.symbols: G = gold documents; R = retrieved candidate list; C = documents that reached the prompt context; the first matching class wins. Sub-flags for generation: citation error (citations miss a gold document) and format error (parse failure).

inputs.other: run trace with candidates and final context

units.range: three shares summing to 1 over the wrong answers
units.higher_is_better: lower generation share means the retriever, not the reader, is the bottleneck; direction depends on what you tune

worked_example.setup: 40 wrong answers out of 100: 22 had a gold document missing from the candidates, 9 had all gold documents retrieved but one dropped before the context, 9 had all gold documents in context. (illustrative)

units.blind_spots: Document-level gold only: a document can be in context while the needed sentence is cut or buried. Multi-hop questions need all gold documents, so the retrieval class dominates by construction. Does not say why generation failed (use reading examples). Alternative valid evidence paths are labelled failures.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Turns recall_at_k and all_hop_recall into an actionable split: if rank/cut is large, raise k or fix the reranker; if generation is large, change the prompt or reader. Complements stage_latency/cost for deciding what to optimise.

source.cite: Course handout (IUST Advanced NLP), student_handout.pdf section 8.4 (automatic error classification)

units.notes: Classification rule read in the handout; the counts are invented. The handout adds graph flags (lost in graph, linking failure, expansion noise).

units.name: Pedagogical dimension scores (MRBench taxonomy)
units.question: Does the tutor response identify the mistake, locate it, avoid giving away the answer, guide, and stay actionable?
units.symbols: d = a dimension: mistake identification, mistake location, revealing of the answer, providing guidance, actionability, coherence, tutor tone, human-likeness (Maurya et al.); l = the three-level label of response i on d. The 0.5 weight is our choice, not the paper's.
units.higher_is_better: higher (note: for 'revealing of the answer', a revealed answer is a negative: reverse-code)

worked_example.setup: 20 tutor responses labelled on mistake identification: Yes 12, To some extent 5, No 3.

units.blind_spots: Labels depend on the judge or annotators; the three-level scale is coarse. A tutor can score well on tone and be wrong. Weighting is ours.
units.use_vs_neighbours: The standard taxonomy for tutor responses (8 dimensions verified in the paper). Use it for the pedagogical comparison of the three arms; add correctness separately.

source.cite: Maurya, Petukhova, Kochmar et al. 2025, Unifying AI Tutor Evaluation: An Evaluation Taxonomy for Pedagogical Ability Assessment of LLM-Powered AI Tutors (NAACL)

units.name: Pedagogical win rate vs reference teacher (MathTutorBench)
units.question: Is the tutor's reply preferred over a reference teacher reply by a trained pedagogy reward model?
units.symbols: R_theta = reward model trained to separate expert from novice teacher replies; x = dialogue context; y = reply.

inputs.llm_judge: yes (reward model, released with the benchmark)

worked_example.setup: 10 dialogue turns; the reward model prefers the system's reply in 6.

units.blind_spots: Math tutoring dialogues, not ML concepts: transfer is unchecked. Reward model has its own bias. Single-turn view of a multi-turn skill.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use as a precedent and as a possible external check of the pedagogical quality. The benchmark also measures problem solving, Socratic questioning and mistake detection (table in the paper).

source.cite: Macina et al. 2025, MathTutorBench

units.name: Key-point checklist score (TutorEval)
units.question: Does the answer cover the points an expert said a good answer must contain?
units.formula_latex: S_q=\frac{1}{|K_q|}\sum_{k\in K_q}\mathbb 1[\text{answer covers key point }k],\quad \mathrm{TutorEval}=\frac1{|Q|}\sum_q S_q
units.symbols: K_q = human-written key points for question q; the judge (GPT-4 in the paper) checks each. The paper's own scale (a graded 1 to 10 scoring against the key points) differs: this is the simplified form for the demo.

worked_example.setup: A question has 4 key points; the answer covers 3.

units.blind_spots: Key points are written by one author; a good alternative explanation can miss them. The judge is GPT-4 (paper reports human-GPT-4 score correlation). Simplified formula here is ours.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Closest published format to our own item design: science textbook questions with expert checklists (834 questions over five fields, 205 of them CS: counts verified in the paper table).

source.cite: Chevalier et al. 2024, Language Models as Science Tutors (ICML)

units.name: Answer leakage rate
units.question: When the tutor should only guide, how often does it hand over the final answer?
units.formula_latex: \mathrm{Leak}=\frac{\#\{\text{tutor turns on guided items that contain the final answer}\}}{N_{\mathrm{guided}}}
units.symbols: Guided items = problems where the pedagogy requires withholding the answer (our restriction); leakage = the tutor reveals the final answer, whether correct or not (Maurya et al. 2025, Table 2); paper labels are yes / to some extent / no, so a binary leak needs a rule for 'to some extent'.

worked_example.setup: 40 turns on guided items; 6 reveal the answer.

units.blind_spots: String matching misses paraphrased leaks; a tutor that never helps scores 0 leakage. Pair with guidance quality.
units.use_vs_neighbours: A tutor-specific safety metric (MRBench has 'revealing of the answer'; EduGuard discussed in [[Agentic RAG in Education]]). Needs a guided-item split in our bank.

source.cite: Maurya et al. 2025 (MRBench taxonomy), 'Revealing of the answer'
source.where: Table 2 (p.4): 'Does the tutor reveal the final answer (whether correct or not)?'; p.6: Desired Annotation Match Rate (DAMR) = share of responses with the desired label; labels are yes / to some extent / no

superseded.text: Guided items = problems where the pedagogy requires withholding the answer; leakage = the gold answer (or a paraphrase) appears in the reply.

units.name: Normalised learning gain (Hake)
units.question: How much of the possible improvement did students achieve between pre-test and post-test?
units.symbols: S_pre, S_post = mean class scores before and after; S_max = maximum score (100). The individual-level version uses each student's own pre and post.

inputs.other: pre/post test scores for each arm

worked_example.setup: Mean pre-test 40, mean post-test 70.

units.blind_spots: Needs a real classroom study (after the offline evaluation). Sensitive to ceiling effects and to test difficulty. Not causal without a control arm.
units.use_vs_neighbours: The outcome the thesis ultimately cares about. Offline proxies (correctness, faithfulness, pedagogy) are only predictions of it, and simulations have diverged from classroom results (LEA, 2026).

source.cite: Hake 1998, Interactive-engagement versus traditional methods, Am. J. Phys. 66(1), 64-74
source.id: doi:10.1119/1.18809 (DOI and bibliographic data confirmed by Crossref on 2026-10-09)
source.where: Eq. (1) and definitions (e)-(g), (PDF p.3): <g> = (%<Sf> - %<Si>) / (100 - %<Si>), class averages; High-g > 0.7, medium-g 0.7 > <g> > 0.3, low-g < 0.3. Read from the author's posted PDF (Wayback copy of web.physics.indiana.edu/sdi/ajpv3i.pdf)

units.name: Cohen's d (effect size between arms)
units.question: How large is the difference between two groups in standard-deviation units?
units.symbols: x-bar = group means; s = group standard deviations; n = group sizes.

inputs.other: per-student scores of two groups

worked_example.setup: Group 1: mean 72, sd 10, n 30. Group 2: mean 66, sd 12, n 30.

units.blind_spots: Depends on the pooled spread; unstable with small groups. Says nothing about significance by itself.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Pair p-values with d in the learning-gain study. Conventional labels (0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large) are rules of thumb.

source.cite: Cohen 1988, Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences, as reproduced in Lakens 2013, Frontiers in Psychology 4:863
source.where: Lakens 2013, Eq. (1): d_s = (mean1 - mean2) / sqrt(((n1-1) SD1^2 + (n2-1) SD2^2) / (n1+n2-2)), attributed to Cohen (1988); Hedges' g correction follows in the same section

units.name: Prerequisite concept coverage (ours)
units.question: Does the answer or explanation mention the prerequisite concepts the knowledge graph says are needed?
units.symbols: C_req = concepts that the KG lists as prerequisites (one or two hops) of the question's target concept; C_ans = concepts present in the answer (matched by the KG's concept names or ids).

inputs.other: the KG and a concept matcher; no gold answer

units.higher_is_better: higher (as a diagnostic, not a goal)

worked_example.setup: Target concept 'backpropagation' has required prerequisites {chain rule, gradient, loss function, computational graph}; the answer mentions 3.

units.blind_spots: Our own proposal, not validated against learning outcomes. Mentioning is not explaining. It favours the graph arm by construction (the KG defines the list): use an independent prerequisite list (LectureBank) to avoid circularity.
units.use_vs_neighbours: A graph-specific educational diagnostic. Report it, but never as the only evidence for GraphRAG.

units.name: Bootstrap confidence interval
units.question: How uncertain is this average score, given only this many questions?
units.symbols: x_i = per-question score; B = number of resamples (1,000 to 10,000); the interval is the 2.5th and 97.5th percentile of the resampled means.

inputs.other: per-question scores

worked_example.setup: 10 per-question scores (1 = correct): 1,1,0,1,0,1,1,0,1,1. Mean = 0.7. Resample 10,000 times (seed 7 in Python).
worked_example.steps: Percentile interval of the resampled means (random seed dependent).

units.blind_spots: Treats questions as independent: the same document in many questions breaks this (use a cluster bootstrap). Tiny n gives wide, unstable intervals.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Report an interval for every headline number. With 300 questions the interval is about plus or minus 5 points for accuracies near 0.6.

source.cite: Efron & Tibshirani 1993, An Introduction to the Bootstrap
source.where: not read (book not available locally). Secondary: Lutkepohl 2011 p.712 (standard percentile interval [s*_(g/2), s*_(1-g/2)], cites Efron & Tibshirani 1993); scipy.stats.bootstrap docs (percentile / basic / BCa, default BCa)

units.name: Cohen's kappa (judge-human agreement)
units.question: Does the LLM judge agree with human labels more than chance would?
units.symbols: p_o = observed share of agreement; p_e = agreement expected by chance from the two raters' label frequencies (J = judge, H = human).

worked_example.setup: 100 items. Both say yes: 40. Judge yes, human no: 10. Judge no, human yes: 5. Both no: 45.

units.blind_spots: Sensitive to class imbalance (paradoxes with rare labels). Needs a sample large enough (about 100 or more).
units.use_vs_neighbours: Report for every LLM judge before using it. 0.6 to 0.8 is usually called substantial (a convention).

source.cite: Cohen 1960, A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales (Educ. Psychol. Meas. 20(1))
source.where: not read (paywalled, no open copy found: Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex report closed access). Secondary: Burkov 2020 Machine Learning Engineering p.145; Eisenstein 2019 Natural Language Processing p.108 Eq. 4.11; scikit-learn cohen_kappa_score (sum0 x sum1 / n expected counts), main branch

units.name: McNemar test (paired arms)
units.question: Is the difference in accuracy between two systems on the same questions bigger than chance?
units.symbols: b = questions system A gets right and B wrong; c = A wrong and B right. Questions both get right or both wrong carry no information.

worked_example.setup: Same 100 questions: A right and B wrong on 15; A wrong and B right on 5.

units.blind_spots: Needs binary correctness. Exact binomial test is better when b + c is small (under 25). Multiple arms and many metrics need a correction for multiple comparisons.
units.use_vs_neighbours: The simple paired test for 'is GraphRAG better than vector RAG on this question set'. Use a paired bootstrap for non-binary scores.

source.cite: Dietterich 1998, Approximate Statistical Tests for Comparing Supervised Classification Learning Algorithms (Neural Computation 10(7)), Section 3.1; the original McNemar 1947 (Psychometrika 12(2)) was not read
source.where: Section 3.1 'McNemar's test', statistic (|n01 - n10| - 1)^2/(n01 + n10), chi-square with 1 d.f., continuity correction of -1 (PDF p.7; read by OCR because the text layer is garbled)

units.name: Paired bootstrap difference between two systems
units.question: Is system B really better than system A on the same questions, or is the gap within noise?
units.formula_latex: \Delta^*_b=\frac1n\sum_{i}\big(b_{i_b}-a_{i_b}\big)\ \ (\text{same resampled indices } i_b\text{ for both systems}),\quad \mathrm{CI}_{95}=[\Delta^*_{(0.025)},\Delta^*_{(0.975)}],\quad p_{\le0}=\frac1B\sum_b\mathbb{1}[\Delta^*_b\le0]
units.symbols: a_i, b_i = per-question scores of systems A and B on the same question i; B = 1000 resamples; indices are drawn once, rng.integers(0, n, size=(B, n)), and reused for both systems; percentiles use linear interpolation.

inputs.other: per-question scores of two systems on the same questions

units.range: a difference with an interval; p_le_zero between 0 and 1
units.higher_is_better: interval excluding 0 on the positive side supports 'B better'

worked_example.setup: 20 questions, EM per question for A and B (A mean 0.50, B mean 0.70). 1000 resamples, seed 0, numpy default_rng.
worked_example.steps: Draw one index matrix, compute mean(B)-mean(A) in each resample, take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles and the share of resamples with difference <= 0.

units.blind_spots: Treats questions as independent (clustered questions need a cluster bootstrap). With about 300 questions an interval around a rate of 0.5 is roughly +-5.7 points, so differences of a few points are not findings. Paired intervals are tighter than two separate intervals only because the same questions are compared; it says nothing about other question sets. Choose hypotheses and the final system before seeing test results, or the p-value is meaningless.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Prefer it to comparing two separate bootstrap_ci intervals (it uses the pairing, so it is more sensitive). McNemar (mcnemar) is the exact test for binary correctness; the paired bootstrap also works for F1, nDCG and any per-question score.

source.cite: Course handout (IUST Advanced NLP), student_handout.pdf section 7.8 and 8.3; method: Efron & Tibshirani 1993

units.notes: Procedure (1000 resamples, seed 0, 95 percent, indices drawn once, p_le_zero) read in the handout; the data are invented. Numbers computed with numpy default_rng(0), as specified there.
